name: Crown of Aragon
summary: A union of Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia and Mallorca with a sea empire in the Mediterranean (Sicily, Sardinia, Naples); joined Castile through Ferdinand and Isabella to form Spain.

knownFor.label: Almogavars
knownFor.note: Light infantry who fought across the Mediterranean.

terrain.value: The Ebro valley, the Pyrenees mountains and a long Mediterranean coast, plus islands such as Mallorca and Sicily.

climate.value: Mediterranean, with hot, dry summers and mild winters, and drier inland.

resources.value: Grain, wine, olive oil, textiles, salt and fish.

disasters.value: The Black Death (1348) killed many in Catalonia, Aragon and Valencia.

population.value: About one million people in the Iberian lands around 1300, with more in Sicily and Sardinia.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; a few walled towns and a royal or ducal capital.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Catalan settlers in Valencia and Mallorca.

economicBase.value: Mediterranean trade, textiles (especially in Barcelona), and farming and herding.

tradeRoutes.value: Barcelona’s Mediterranean trade reached Sicily, North Africa, Constantinople and Italy; Barcelona’s consulate of the sea set maritime law.

wealth.value: Merchants and bankers in Barcelona and Valencia grew rich on trade.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold florins are mentioned; the article does not mention croats.

inequality.value: Nobles and clergy above peasants, many of them serfs.

governmentType.value: Union of realms under one king, each with its own laws.

keyRulers.value: James I the Conqueror (no reign dates in the article). Peter III. Ferdinand II (reign 1479–1516 per the infobox).

succession.value: Martin I died in 1410 without living heirs; representatives chose Ferdinand of Antequera (the Compromise of Caspe; no date in the article).

institutions.value: A Diputación del General was set up in each realm, becoming the Generalitat in Catalonia and Valencia (undated in the article).

stability.value: The Catalan civil war (1462–72) broke out between the crown and the Catalan elite.

eliteConflict.value: Nobles and towns, represented in the Cortes (parliaments), resisted royal power and demanded rights.

armyAndTech.value: A strong navy, and the Almogavars, hardy light infantry who fought in Sicily and Greece.

majorWars.value: Conquest of Mallorca (established 1231 per the article’s table) and of Valencia (1238–1245 per the infobox); Peter III’s war after the Sicilian Vespers (1282).

territoryChange.value: Sicily annexed in 1282 (lost in 1713); the Kingdom of Sardinia created in 1297 and conquered from 1324; Naples taken by Alfonso V in 1442.

alliancesRivals.value: France and Genoa were the main rivals in the Mediterranean; Castile was both a rival and later a partner.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; Catalan mapmakers produced the Catalan Atlas (1375).

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Roads, rivers and Mediterranean shipping carried goods and people.

religion.value: Catholic Christianity, with sizeable Muslim and Jewish minorities, especially in Valencia and Aragon.

languageWriting.value: Catalan, Aragonese and Latin were written, and Catalan literature flourished.

artsArchitecture.value: Catalan Gothic buildings such as Barcelona’s Santa Maria del Mar and Valencia’s Silk Exchange.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the crown, the Church and each kingdom’s own laws and customs.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

neighbours.value: Castile, Navarre, France and the Muslim kingdom of Granada.

ideasReligions.value: The Union of Aragon (1283) forced the king to confirm the privileges of nobles and towns (the article does not use the term “pactism”).

colonisation.value: A Mediterranean island empire: Mallorca, Sicily, Sardinia, and later Naples.

riseSignals.value: Union with Barcelona: the body dates the origin to 1137; the infobox gives 1162.

peakPeriod.value: A sea empire in the 1200s–1300s: Sicily from 1282, Sardinia from 1297.

declineSignals.value: The Black Death, plague and civil war weakened the realm before union with Castile in 1479.

outcome.value: Dynastic union with Castile (1479 in the lead); consolidation under Charles I in 1516.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
